summary: Pupils aged 11–12 observe, interpret and record real cell structure using a light microscope, discovering through evidence that all living things are made of cells. The core experience is preparing/viewing slides (onion epidermis, cheek cells, pond water), distinguishing genuine structures (nucleus, cytoplasm, membrane) from artefacts (air bubbles, fibres, stain blobs), and recording observations as a labelled biological drawing. The load-bearing conceptual outcome is the evidence-based generalisation 'all living things are made of cells'. Keep organelle detail light; structure functions come later.
misconceptions: Thinking cells are only in 'some' living things (e.g. animals but not plants, or not in oneself), rather than the universal unit of life.
Interpreting artefacts — air bubbles, stain blobs, fibres — as cell structures.
Believing cells are the size of things you can see with the naked eye, missing the scale (crosscutting: phenomena at one scale not observable at another).
Assuming the microscope 'makes' the cells rather than revealing structures that were always there.
Confusing a single cell with a whole organism, or thinking a drawn textbook cell is exactly what every real cell looks like.

activities.title: Simulated microscope: focus, observe, interpret, record
steps: Clip a slide (start with onion epidermis) onto the stage and begin from a blurred view.

At low power, turn the coarse focus, overshoot, then ease the fine focus until the cells come into sharp focus — a grid of brick-shaped plant cells, many showing a nucleus (clearly dark when stained, e.g. with iodine).
Increase the magnification and observe how individual cells appear larger and show more internal detail (nucleus, cytoplasm) while fewer cells fit in the field of view.
Swap specimens to your own cheek cells (rounder, no cell wall) and to pond water containing single-celled organisms, gathering evidence specimen by specimen.
Decide, for a seeded air bubble and a stray fibre in the field, which marks are real cell structures and which are artefacts — do NOT label the bubble or fibre as a cell.

Tag the nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane (in onion cells the visible outline is mainly the cell wall, with the membrane pressed just inside it and usually not seen separately), then sketch what you actually see into a recording/drawing panel using clear lines, no shading, with labels.
activities.insight: Most cells are too small to see with the naked eye; the microscope reveals the hidden building blocks of life. Across different specimens — plant, animal, microbe — every living thing examined turns out to be made of cells, supporting the generalisation that all living things are made of cells.

activities.title: Real bench microscope slide work
steps: Where lab access allows, prepare a wet-mount slide of onion epidermis and/or stained cheek cells.
Start on the lowest-power objective, focus using coarse then fine adjustment, and use only fine focus at higher power while observing the real specimen.
Identify nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane in the live view (in onion cells the visible outline is mainly the cell wall; the membrane is pressed against it and usually not distinguishable).
Produce a labelled biological drawing of the cells you observe.
activities.insight: Working with a genuine specimen is the real goal: the cells you see are actual structures in actual tissue, reinforcing that living material is built from cells.

activities.title: Annotated micrograph gallery across organisms
steps: Examine annotated micrographs of onion and cheek cells; reveal the names of nucleus, cytoplasm and membrane.
Work through a 'bubble or cell?' comparison, deciding which image shows a real structure.
Browse a gallery of cells from different organisms (e.g. human skin, leaf, blood) to build the idea that big living things, not only microbes, are built from cells.
activities.insight: A single labelled diagram is not exactly what every real cell looks like; across many organisms the common finding is that all are made of cells.

activities.title: Consolidation checks: structure, name and artefact
steps: Match each structure to its name (nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane).
Choose which of several images is an air-bubble artefact rather than a cell.
Trace the outline of the cell membrane around an animal cell (e.g. a cheek cell) in a micrograph.
activities.insight: Secure recognition of named structures and reliable discrimination of real cells from artefacts.

activities.title: Enrichment: the micrograph is a slice of a 3D cell
steps: Explore a rotatable 3D onion or cheek cell and relate it to the flat micrograph.
Describe how the microscope view is a thin optical section of a three-dimensional object.
activities.insight: Cells are not flat, empty boxes; the flat image is one slice through a three-dimensional structure.

checkQuestion: You looked at onion skin under the microscope and saw a grid of little boxes — cells. Is a slice of your own skin, or a leaf on a tree, also made of cells like that? And if we're all made of cells, why can't you see them just by looking at your hand?
checkAnswer: Yes — all living things, including plants, animals and you, are made of cells; the onion, the leaf and your own skin are all built from cells. You can't see them with the naked eye because cells are microscopic, far too small to see without magnification, which is why a microscope is needed.
